question_text: A 65-year-old man presents to the physician for the evaluation of increasing dyspnea and swelling of the lower extremities over the past year. He has no cough. He also complains of frequent awakenings at night and excessive daytime sleepiness. He has no history of a serious illness. He takes no medications other than zolpidem before sleep. He is a 35-pack-year smoker. His blood pressure is 155/95 mm Hg. His BMI is 37 kg/m2. Oropharyngeal examination shows a small orifice and an enlarged tongue and uvula. The soft palate is low-lying. The examination of the nasal cavity shows no septal deviation or polyps. Symmetric pitting edema is seen below the knee, bilaterally. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Echocardiography shows a mildly dilated right ventricle and an elevated systolic pulmonary artery pressure with no abnormalities of the left heart. A ventilation-perfusion scan shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms?

                    ### Question

The examination of the nasal cavity shows no septal deviation or polyps. Symmetric pitting edema is seen below the knee, bilaterally. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Echocardiography shows a mildly dilated right ventricle and an elevated systolic pulmonary artery pressure with no abnormalities of the left heart. A ventilation-perfusion scan shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
opb. Heart failure with a preserved ejection fraction
opc. Idiopathic pulmonary artery hypertension
opd. Obstructive sleep apnea
ope. Pulmonary thromboembolism

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient's symptoms are most consistent with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). OSA is characterized by intermittent hypoxia due to upper airway obstruction during sleep, leading to pulmonary vasoconstriction and elevated pulmonary artery pressure, which can cause right ventricular dilation. This aligns with the echocardiography findings of a mildly dilated right ventricle and elevated systolic pulmonary artery pressure. The patient's obesity and enlarged oropharyngeal structures further support the diagnosis of OSA. Additionally, OSA can cause frequent awakenings at night, excessive daytime sleepiness, and increased blood pressure, all of which are present in this patient. The retrieved evidence paths broadly associate dyspnea and edema with heart failure, but the absence of left heart abnormalities and the presence of right heart strain in this patient make OSA a more likely cause. Idiopathic pulmonary artery hypertension and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction are less likely due to the specific clinical presentation and lack of left heart involvement.
